lead: Two numbers describe every second-order circuit. The natural frequency ω<sub>n</sub> (rad/s) says how fast the circuit would oscillate with no energy loss. The damping ratio ζ (no unit) says how strongly resistance kills that oscillation. From them you get the pole positions, the ringing frequency, the overshoot, the peak time and the settling time. Designers use this language for filters, speaker crossovers, control loops and power supplies, where ringing wastes time and can trip protection. You can tune L and C for ω<sub>n</sub> and R for ζ.
prereq: You need: second-order RLC circuits for the characteristic equation and the three damping cases.

sections.h3: Two numbers replace the component values

blocks.text: A second-order circuit has two storage elements, so its characteristic equation is quadratic. Write it with two numbers: the natural frequency ω<sub>n</sub> and the damping ratio ζ. The symbol s is the complex frequency in s⁻¹. ω<sub>n</sub>, in rad/s, is the frequency the circuit would oscillate at if no energy were lost. ζ, with no unit, is how strongly energy loss kills that oscillation.

blocks.where: s is the complex frequency in s⁻¹; ω<sub>n</sub> is the natural frequency in rad/s; ζ is the damping ratio (no unit).

blocks.text: For a series RLC, ωn = 1/√(LC) and α = R/(2L), where α is the neper frequency in s⁻¹. For a parallel RLC, α = 1/(2RC). Then ζ = α/ωn. Do not use the series α in a parallel circuit; each α belongs to its own topology. ωn is the same number as the ω₀ of second-order RLC circuits; some syllabi call ζ the damping factor. A useful inverse is Q = 1/(2ζ); high Q means light damping and a long ring. These two numbers are not extra components; they are a relabelling of R, L and C.

Solve the characteristic equation for the poles: s = −ζω<sub>n</sub> ± ω<sub>n</sub>√(ζ² − 1). The square root changes character at ζ = 1. For ζ < 1 it is imaginary, so the roots are complex conjugates. Rewrite them as s = −ζω<sub>n</sub> ± jω_n√(1 − ζ²). The real part −ζω<sub>n</sub> is negative; its size ζω<sub>n</sub> = α, in s⁻¹, is the decay rate of the envelope e<sup>−ζω<sub>n</sub> t</sup>. The imaginary part is the damped frequency ω<sub>d</sub> = ω<sub>n</sub>√(1 − ζ²) rad/s. The circuit rings at ω<sub>d</sub>, not at ω<sub>n</sub>. The two differ for every ζ > 0, but only slightly when ζ is small: at ζ = 0.1 the difference is 0.5 %.
s is the complex pole in s⁻¹; ζ is the damping ratio; ω<sub>n</sub> is the natural frequency in rad/s; ω<sub>d</sub> is the damped frequency in rad/s; j = √(−1).

At ζ = 1 the two roots meet at s = −ω<sub>n</sub>. For ζ > 1 both roots are real and negative. At ζ = 0 the roots sit on the jω axis and the oscillation never dies. A negative ζ puts a root in the right half-plane and the response grows. The common error is to write ω<sub>d</sub> = ω<sub>n</sub>√(ζ² − 1); that expression is imaginary for ζ < 1 and is not a measurable frequency.

Step-response specifications follow from the same two numbers. Percentage overshoot is the largest rise above the final value: overshoot = 100 e<sup>−πζ/√(1−ζ²)</sup> %. Peak time t<sub>p</sub> = π/ω<sub>d</sub> seconds is when the first peak occurs. The 2 % settling time t<sub>s</sub> ≈ 4/(ζω<sub>n</sub>) seconds is when the envelope has fallen to about 2 % of its starting size. These formulas assume the standard second-order low-pass response, such as the capacitor voltage of a series RLC, with zero initial energy and a step input. They are estimates when the circuit has zeros.

M<sub>p</sub> is percentage overshoot; ζ is the damping ratio; ω<sub>d</sub> is the damped frequency in rad/s; t<sub>p</sub> is peak time in s; t<sub>s</sub> is 2 % settling time in s; ω<sub>n</sub> is the natural frequency in rad/s.

Use them to choose L and C for ωn and R for ζ. In a series circuit, raising R raises α and ζ, so ringing dies faster but the response creeps once ζ passes 1. In a parallel circuit, raising R lowers α and ζ, so a large parallel resistor lets the tank ring longer. On the s-plane the poles lie on a circle of radius ωn and move along it as ζ changes; network functions reads that picture.

figure.caption: Poles of a circuit with ωₙ = 1000 rad/s for four damping ratios. Underdamped poles sit on the dashed circle of radius ωₙ: the worked example (ζ = 0.1) has its pair at −100 ± j995, so it decays at 100 s⁻¹ and rings at 995 rad/s. At ζ = 1 the pair meets at −1000; above 1 they split along the real axis.

examples.question: A series RLC circuit has R = 20 Ω, L = 0.1 H and C = 10 μF. A 10 V step is applied at t = 0 with zero initial energy. Find ω<sub>n</sub>, α, ζ, ω<sub>d</sub>, percentage overshoot, peak time and 2 % settling time.
steps: Compute LC = (0.1 H)(10 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 1 × 10⁻⁶ s². Then ω<sub>n</sub> = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(1 × 10⁻⁶) = 1000 rad/s.
For a series RLC, α = R/(2L) = 20 Ω/(2 × 0.1 H) = 100 s⁻¹.
ζ = α/ω<sub>n</sub> = 100/1000 = 0.1. The circuit is underdamped.
examples.answer: ω<sub>n</sub> = 1000 rad/s, α = 100 s⁻¹, ζ = 0.1, ω<sub>d</sub> ≈ 995 rad/s, overshoot ≈ 72.9 %, t<sub>p</sub> ≈ 3.16 ms and t<sub>s</sub> ≈ 40 ms.
examples.check:
import math
R = 20.0
L = 0.1
C = 10e-6
wn = 1.0 / math.sqrt(L * C)
alpha = R / (2.0 * L)
zeta = alpha / wn
wd = wn * math.sqrt(1.0 - zeta * zeta)
mp = 100.0 * math.exp(-math.pi * zeta / math.sqrt(1.0 - zeta * zeta))
tp_ms = (math.pi / wd) * 1000.0
ts_ms = (4.0 / (zeta * wn)) * 1000.0
print(f'{wn:.0f}')
print(f'{alpha:.0f}')
print(f'{zeta:.1f}')
print(f'{wd:.0f}')
print(f'{mp:.1f}')
print(f'{tp_ms:.2f}')
print(f'{ts_ms:.0f}')

traps: Using ω<sub>d</sub> = ω<sub>n</sub>√(ζ² − 1) for an underdamped circuit; it is imaginary when ζ < 1.
Feeding the parallel α = 1/(2RC) into a series RLC, or the series α = R/(2L) into a parallel RLC.
Forgetting that ζ is dimensionless while α is in s⁻¹; ζ = α/ω<sub>n</sub> needs both in the same units.
Applying overshoot and settling formulas to a circuit with zeros or nonzero initial energy without checking the standard second-order assumptions.

quiz.q: Define natural frequency ω<sub>n</sub> and damping ratio ζ for a second-order circuit.
quiz.a: ω<sub>n</sub> is the frequency in rad/s at which the circuit would oscillate with no loss. ζ is the dimensionless ratio ζ = α/ω<sub>n</sub>, where α is the neper frequency in s⁻¹.

quiz.q: Write ω<sub>n</sub> and α for a series RLC.
quiz.a: ω<sub>n</sub> = 1/√(LC) rad/s and α = R/(2L) s⁻¹.

quiz.q: Why is the damped frequency ω<sub>d</sub> less than ω<sub>n</sub> for 0 < ζ < 1?
quiz.a: The resistive term opposes the movement of charge and weakens the net restoring effect, so each swing takes a little longer. In numbers, ω<sub>d</sub> = √(ω<sub>n</sub>² − α²), which is below ω<sub>n</sub> whenever α > 0; at ζ = 0, ω<sub>d</sub> = ω<sub>n</sub>.

quiz.q: A series RLC has R = 40 Ω, L = 0.1 H and C = 10 μF. Find ω<sub>n</sub>, α and ζ.
For ω<sub>n</sub> = 1000 rad/s and ζ = 0.6, find ω<sub>d</sub> and the percentage overshoot.
In a parallel RLC, why does increasing R lower ζ and make ringing last longer?
quiz.a: For a parallel RLC, α = 1/(2RC). Increasing R lowers α. Since ζ = α/ω<sub>n</sub>, ζ also falls, so the decay rate ζω<sub>n</sub> is smaller and the oscillation takes longer to die.

quiz.q: Two circuits have the same ω<sub>n</sub> but ζ = 0.05 and ζ = 0.7. Compare their overshoot and settling time.
quiz.a: The ζ = 0.05 circuit has much larger overshoot and rings for many cycles; its settling time is about 4/(0.05ω<sub>n</sub>) = 80/ω<sub>n</sub>. The ζ = 0.7 circuit settles in about 4/(0.7ω<sub>n</sub>) ≈ 5.7/ω<sub>n</sub> and has small overshoot.

beyond: Not for the exam. Control engineers describe motors and drones with the same ζ and ω<sub>n</sub>, then add zeros and delays that the formulas here ignore. Filter designers trade Q against component tolerance because a high-Q tank rings after every supply dip. Power-supply loops use damping to stop output overshoot from tripping a phone's protection chip. Search next for second-order system step response, pole-zero placement, and RLC quality factor.
